items.title: Place value and comparison
items.content: In a decimal, places to the right are tenths, hundredths, thousandths, and so on. Compare whole parts first, then align decimal places with zeros.

items.title: Operations and rounding
items.content: Addition/subtraction: align decimal points. Multiplication: multiply as whole numbers, then place the decimal using the total decimal digits. Division: shift both numbers equally to make the divisor whole. Round by checking the next digit.

items.title: Exam checks
items.content:
Use estimation to catch a misplaced decimal point.
A trailing zero changes appearance, not the number’s value.

items.title: Read and compare decimals
items.content: Worked example: compare 4.7 and 4.68. Write 4.70 and 4.68; hence \(4.70>4.68\). Trailing zeros do not change value.

items.title: Add and subtract
items.content: Worked example: \(12.45+3.8=12.45+3.80=16.25\). For subtraction, align the same way: \(8.00-2.37=5.63\).

items.title: Multiply decimals
items.content: Worked example: \(2.4\times0.35\): calculate \(24\times35=840\); three decimal places total, so answer is 0.840 = 0.84.

items.title: Divide decimals
items.content: Worked example: \(5.76/0.12\). Multiply both by 100: \(576/12=48\).

items.title: Rounding and estimation
items.content: Worked example: round 18.746 to 2 decimal places. The third decimal is 6, so 18.74 rounds up to 18.75. Estimate \(19\times0.5\approx9.5\) to check a result.

items.title: Decimals as fractions and money
items.content: Worked example: \(0.375=375/1000=3/8\). Money calculations should retain the currency unit and usually round to the nearest paise only at the end.

items.title: Compare or order decimals
items.content: Append zeros to align places, then compare digits. Worked example: order 2.09, 2.9, 2.099: write 2.090, 2.900, 2.099; order is 2.09 < 2.099 < 2.9.

items.title: Calculate with decimal measures
items.content: Align decimal points for addition/subtraction and state the resulting unit. Worked example: 3.6 m + 85 cm = 3.6 m + 0.85 m = 4.45 m.

items.title: Scale or unit-price word problem
items.content: Worked example: 1.25 kg costs ₹80/kg; cost is \(1.25\times80=₹100\).

items.title: Round to required precision
items.content: Worked example: 7.385 to two decimal places is 7.39 because the next digit is 5; follow the stated rounding convention.

items.title: Why decimal addition aligns places
items.content: Tenths can be added to tenths and hundredths to hundredths, just as like units are combined. Rewriting 3.8 as 3.80 makes place values line up.

items.title: Why decimal multiplication counts places
items.content: A decimal with one place is tenths and one with two places is hundredths. Their product has denominator \(10\times100=1000\), so the product has three decimal places before simplification.

items.title: Why shifting in decimal division preserves the quotient
items.content: Multiplying dividend and divisor by the same nonzero power of 10 leaves their ratio unchanged: \(a/b=(10^ka)/(10^kb)\).

sections.title: Common errors and how to avoid them

items.title: Misaligning decimal points
items.content: Align the points for addition and subtraction; never align the last digits.

items.title: Placing product decimal by appearance
items.content: Count total decimal places in both factors after multiplication.

items.title: Moving only one number in division
items.content: Shift the dividend and divisor by the same number of places.

items.title: Rounding too early
items.content: Keep full precision until the final requested rounding step.

keyTakeaways: Align decimal places for addition and subtraction.
Move both numbers equally when dividing.
Round only at the requested place value.
